title: SUMIF with a Date Range
description: SUMIF only takes one condition, so summing between two dates needs a trick. Learn three clean ways to SUMIF (or SUMIFS) over a date range in Excel and Google Sheets.
intro: A very common question is "how do I SUMIF the amounts where the date is between Jan 1 and Mar 31?" Because SUMIF accepts a single criterion, a single date range isn't enough. This guide shows three patterns — two SUMIFs, the modern SUMIFS, and a SUMPRODUCT fallback — so you can total by any date window.
prerequisites: Dates stored as real Excel dates (not text)
A column of dates and a column of values to sum
Microsoft 365 only needed for dynamic array tricks

sections.title: The Problem with One SUMIF
sections.content: SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range) compares the whole range to a single test. To capture a window you need BOTH a lower bound and an upper bound, which is two criteria — so a single SUMIF can't do it alone.
tips: Confirm your dates are real serial numbers: a date formatted as text won't compare correctly.

sections.title: Method 1: Two SUMIFs (Subtract the Upper Bound)
sections.content: Sum everything from the start date, then subtract everything after the end date. The difference is the window. This works in every version.

steps.name: Sum from start
steps.text: Include all dates on or after the start.

steps.name: Subtract after end
steps.text: Remove dates after the window's last day.

example.result: Total of column B where date is 1 Jan – 31 Mar 2024
example.explanation: The second SUMIF excludes the end day, so use 31 Mar as the cutoff; rows on 31 Mar are kept in the first sum and removed by the second.

tips: Use ">=" for the start and ">" (strictly greater) for the end so the last day is included.

sections.title: Method 2: SUMIFS (Cleanest, Excel 2007+/Sheets)
sections.content: SUMIFS handles multiple criteria natively, so the same lower/upper pair becomes two simple conditions in one function.

example.result: Total of column B for dates 1 Jan – 31 Mar 2024 (inclusive)
example.explanation: Both bounds are inclusive here, which is usually what a report wants.

tips: SUMIFS is generally faster and easier to read than the two-SUMIF trick.

sections.title: Method 3: SUMPRODUCT (Maximum Control)
sections.content: SUMPRODUCT multiplies arrays, so you can express the date window as TRUE/FALSE math and even combine it with other conditions.

example.result: Total of column B for the same quarter
example.explanation: Each condition returns 1/0; only rows where both are 1 contribute their B value.

tips: Restrict to your data range (A2:A1000) instead of whole columns to keep SUMPRODUCT fast.

summary: To SUMIF over a date range, remember that one criterion isn't enough. The two-SUMIF subtraction works everywhere, SUMIFS is the cleanest modern choice, and SUMPRODUCT gives you the most flexibility when you start mixing in extra conditions. Prefer SUMIFS for new work.
